title: Bulleted advice-list items
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic bullet-point style recommendations, typically formatted as 'Bolded Label**: advice sentence' or a terse imperative/tip within a numbered or bulleted self-help/how-to list (e.g., 'Network and build relationships**:', 'Look for error fares**:', 'Set a budget**:', 'Personalize it**:'). It activates most strongly on the concise, actionable tip fragments themselves—advice on networking, gift-giving, budgeting, travel deals, seeking support, and similar practical life-advice topics—regardless of the specific subject matter, because the shared feature is the list-item advice format rather than content. It does not activate on narrative prose, direct quoted dialogue without list formatting, questions posed conversationally (though some clarifying questions in lists partially trigger it), or purely factual/technical statements lacking the imperative 'tip' phrasing and bolded-label structure.

title: Validating and empowering reassurance
description: This latent fires on formulaic, advice-genre closing statements that reassure the reader their feelings, boundaries, or needs are valid and that they have the right/permission to prioritize themselves ('your feelings are valid,' 'it's okay to prioritize your own needs,' 'you're an adult and it's your choice'). It activates most strongly on direct second-person affirmations using stock phrases like 'remember,' 'you deserve,' 'you have the right,' 'it's okay to,' and 'you're not alone,' typically appearing as a summarizing or encouraging tag-on sentence in relationship/self-help style responses. It is weaker or absent on sentences that give concrete advice, describe actions to take, discuss other people's perspectives/compromise, or make conditional/evaluative statements (e.g., 'it may be time to reevaluate,' 'try to find a middle ground') rather than directly affirming the reader's own emotional legitimacy and autonomy.

title: Advice-list discourse markers
description: This latent fires on the structural scaffolding of advice-giving and self-help style text: transitional/hedging connectives like 'However,' that introduce caveats or additional considerations, numbered-list openers ('1.', '**1.'), bolded advice headers ('Take a deep breath**:', 'Be specific and objective.'), and suggested conversational openers phrased as questions ('Could we discuss...?', 'Can you help us out with this?'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic fragments that signal the start of a list item, a qualifying transition, or a suggested phrase to say to someone, rather than on the substantive content of the advice itself. It does not activate on plain narrative or descriptive sentences that lack this list/transition/suggested-dialogue scaffolding, nor on fully fleshed-out explanatory sentences that don't begin with a discourse marker, bold header, or quoted prompt.

title: Empathetic conversational validation and list scaffolding in advice text
description: This latent fires on the discourse-management and rapport-building scaffolding typical of chatbot-style advice/relationship responses: short validating phrases ('That's understandable,' 'That's totally relatable!', 'You're not being unreasonable'), reassurance/normalizing statements ('That's completely normal and healthy'), transitional or hedging connectives ('However,', 'It's important to note that'), and list/enumeration markers ('1.', '2. **', 'Here are some ideas:'). It activates on the structural and tonal glue of advice-giving prose—validating the user's feelings, softening criticism, introducing caveats, or numbering suggestions—rather than on the substantive content of the advice itself. It would not activate on purely factual or narrative sentences lacking this conversational scaffolding (e.g. plain declarative facts, technical descriptions, or content with no reassurance/list/transition markers), even if topically similar to the advice being given.

title: Interpersonal-advice validation statements
description: This latent fires on declarative sentences in advice/relationship-column style text that assess, validate, or characterize a person's situation, feelings, or behavior—e.g., stating that something is 'understandable,' 'unreasonable,' 'hurtful,' 'a red flag,' or 'not your fault.' It activates on second- and third-person evaluative summaries that frame someone's actions or emotions in a judgmental or empathetic register, often as part of a numbered or bulleted breakdown of a conflict situation (financial, relational, or social). It does not activate on neutral factual statements, procedural instructions lacking evaluative framing, direct questions, or list headers/formatting artifacts unless paired with this kind of interpersonal judgment or validation language.

title: Empathetic advice-column validation language
description: This latent fires on the stock rhetorical and validating phrases characteristic of advice-column or chatbot counseling responses: exclamatory acknowledgments ('What a great question!', 'What a thoughtful gesture!', 'Congratulations!', 'The age-old conundrum of...'), empathetic openers ('I'm so sorry to hear that...', 'Wow, that's quite a story!'), and formulaic advice about communicating needs, setting boundaries, or considering alternatives ('Communicate assertively', 'Consider alternative solutions', 'It's your body, your choice'). It activates on short, often bolded or exclamatory framing/validation lines that precede or punctuate interpersonal advice, rather than on the substantive content of the advice itself. It does NOT activate on purely factual, narrative, or descriptive sentences lacking this validating/rhetorical framing, nor on advice content stated in a flat, non-exclamatory, non-empathetic register (e.g. plain instructions or lists without acknowledging phrases).

title: Empathetic validation in advice-giving
description: This latent fires on advice-column-style language that validates the reader's feelings, situation, or actions—phrases like 'it's natural to feel...', 'that's completely understandable', 'you were simply trying to...', or summarizing the person's behavior as reasonable, kind, or justified. It activates on sentences that reassure, normalize emotions, reframe someone's conduct sympathetically, or offer supportive acknowledgment before giving guidance (often in relationship/interpersonal-conflict advice contexts, e.g. AITA-style responses). It also extends to related judgmental framings that label others' behavior as unacceptable, manipulative, or inappropriate, since these often co-occur with validating the reader. It would NOT activate on neutral factual statements, procedural instructions without emotional framing, or purely informational content (e.g. 'check for bundle deals', 'provide proof of identity') that lacks any validating/empathetic or interpersonal-judgment stance.

title: Hedged empathetic judgment in interpersonal advice
description: This latent activates on clauses that render a balanced, softened evaluation of someone's behavior in an interpersonal conflict—acknowledging validity or good intent while still pointing out a fault or shortcoming (e.g. 'not unreasonable,' 'understandable, but...,' 'well-intentioned... not the best approach'). It fires strongly on the hedging/validating language typical of relationship-advice or mediation responses that soften criticism or affirm feelings before or after delivering a judgment. It also picks up on quoted rhetorical accusatory questions ('Did you want it?', 'Can't you read?') embedded in such advice contexts, likely because they serve the same function of citing the other party's behavior for evaluation. It would not activate on purely factual, neutral statements, unhedged blunt judgments without softening language, or advice-adjacent text that lacks this diplomatic validate-then-critique structure.

title: Reddit AITA-style reassurance and framing
description: This latent fires on the stock conversational scaffolding used in Reddit advice/AITA-style responses: greeting formulas ('Welcome to Reddit!'), the acronym/question 'WIBTA?', reassuring verdicts ('You're not the asshole here', 'You're not alone in this feeling'), and wry framing phrases that name a recurring dilemma ('The age-old conundrum of...', 'The classic Am I the Asshole?'). It activates on short, formulaic, validating or scene-setting lines that a chatbot or Redditor uses to open, reassure, or label a personal-advice situation, rather than on the substantive advice or reasoning itself. It does not activate on sentences that give concrete, content-specific advice, factual explanations, or narrative details without this reassuring/labeling framing (e.g., detailed reasoning about a specific action, factual statements, or plain descriptions lacking the validating or 'welcome/age-old' rhetorical template).

title: Empathetic chatbot conversational scaffolding
description: This latent fires on the stock rhetorical moves of a supportive, therapy-style chatbot response: short validating exclamations ('That's fascinating!', 'That's awesome!', 'That takes courage.'), empathetic framing of the user's situation ('That sounds really tough', 'Decision-making can be overwhelming'), follow-up probing questions ('Can you tell me more about...?', 'What specific characteristics...?'), and structural discourse markers that organize advice ('However...', 'Instead,', numbered list openers like '1.', '2. **', 'Here's a suggestion:'). It activates on sentences that perform conversational/emotional scaffolding around a user's disclosure—acknowledging feelings, softening transitions, or introducing enumerated recommendations—regardless of the specific topic (relationships, anxiety, decisions, K-pop, etc). It would not activate on purely factual, narrative, or technical statements that lack this validating/organizing conversational function, e.g. plain descriptions of events or neutral informational content without an empathetic or list-structuring frame.
